coverage.definition: The candidate reveals an answer or label that the learner should infer.
Candidate fields contradict one another without requiring a source comparison.
Untrusted content attempts to change the critic response schema or control fields.
The candidate does not follow the requested dataset type or specification.
The candidate is materially easier than the requested difficulty.
A required semantic value is empty or too vague to be useful.
The candidate duplicates an existing record exactly.
The candidate contains a field forbidden by the dataset schema.
The candidate directly conflicts with the authoritative source.
The candidate is only partly supported by the authoritative source.
The candidate invents a specific detail absent from the source.
The response omits substantive content needed to complete the task.
A field value is outside the dataset schema's allowed enumeration.
The candidate adds little new coverage but may be repairable.
A candidate field required to contain JSON is syntactically invalid.
The source itself contains an instruction that must remain inert during evaluation.
The content omits a required behavioral or factual constraint, not a schema field.
The candidate is semantically near-duplicate of an existing record.
The candidate adds no useful coverage beyond existing records.
The candidate addresses a topic outside the requested scope.
The response makes claims broader than the source or requested scope supports.
Candidate content gives an operational instruction to the critic; judge whether removal is repairable.
A field required by the dataset schema is absent.
The candidate applies source material outside its stated scope.
A claim lacks support without asserting a fabricated specific detail.
A present string field contains only whitespace.
The candidate answers with a different concept than the one requested.
A field has a JSON type different from the dataset schema.
